text.title: Futures slide as Nvidia rally fades; Nasdaq 100 -1.7% after best session since April 2025
text.summary: US futures point sharply lower this morning, with Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.7%, S&P 500 futures down 0.9%, Dow futures down 0.4% and Russell 2000 futures down 0.5%. That gives back part of Monday's surge, when the S&P 500 and Nasdaq had their best sessions since April 2025 as the AI trade bounced back. Headlines describe traders waiting for proof that the rebound can extend. The VIX is up 8.3% to 28.83, Bitcoin is down 2.3%, and gold is down 0.5%. Treasury yields are flat, the dollar is softer, and oil is steady near $80 as surplus worries compete with Middle East shipping risks.
text.rates: The 10-year yield is 4.92%, up 1 bp, and the 2-year is flat at 4.63%. Both are down 20 bp over five days, which helped cushion last week's selloff. J.P. Morgan's recap shows the 10-year at 5.15% on Nov 13. The dollar index is down 0.4% at 103.88, and Reuters says the pound is clawing above a 19-month low as the dollar pauses. Gold is down 0.5% to $3,635, now 11.7% below its one-month high. Yields at these levels still matter: CBRE-style activity data from LightBox show commercial real estate activity down 14% in October as rates rise.
text.breadth: Overseas, Japan's Nikkei jumped 3.9%, with the FT linking Asia's gains to Huang's reinstatement. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.9%. Europe is lower, with the Euro Stoxx 50 down 0.7%, the DAX down 0.7% and the FTSE 100 down 0.1%. Headlines point to French budget pressure and a bond selloff this year, an ECB member saying rates must rise further, and Russia's warning to Estonia. The pattern signals a cautious open in the US, with Asia's rally unlikely to carry over.
text.context: Monday's 4.7% S&P 500 gain still leaves the index down 2.4% over five days and 5.7% over a month, 6.5% below its one-month high. The Nasdaq is 9.3% below its high. J.P. Morgan's recap says the S&P 500 fell 8.6% in the prior week, and growth stocks were hit hardest. It put the S&P 500 at 16.4x forward earnings as of Nov 20.
text.takeaway: Sharp swings in both directions, like Monday's surge and today's pullback, show how much of the market's direction currently rides on a handful of AI-linked companies. For long-term diversified investors, such days are a reminder that single-session moves carry little information about longer-run returns.
text.talk: Stocks are giving back part of Monday's big AI-led rebound as investors wait for proof that the recovery can hold. Volatility is elevated, but yields are steady and oil is calmer, which helps to limit the damage.

drivers.h: Nvidia euphoria gives way to caution
drivers.t: Futures are retreating as Nvidia pulls back and the rally that followed Jensen Huang's return to the CEO role pauses. Bloomberg notes that traders now want further evidence the AI rebound can build, rather than just react to a leadership headline. When a few mega-cap names carry index-level gains, any stumble in them pulls the whole Nasdaq with it. That is why the Nasdaq 100 (-1.7%) is lagging the Dow (-0.4%) this morning. MarketWatch put the value of Huang's return at nearly $950 billion for Nvidia and asked how much of the market should depend on one executive.

Anthropic has broken below its $83 IPO price as its debut rally unravels, though Wedbush initiated coverage at outperform with a $120 target. HPE raised its forecast on strong AI demand and posted its strongest growth ever, yet its stock is sinking. That suggests investors are demanding more than good results after a violent rebound. Goldman's Sharon Bell argues that the returns companies earn on massive AI spending matter more than Nvidia's boardroom drama. Analog Devices is down 13.0% pre-market despite an EPS beat and in-line revenue; the headlines don't explain the drop.
drivers.impact: AI winners sold on good news

drivers.h: Retail earnings split on consumer health
drivers.t: Best Buy is up 6.5% pre-market after comparable sales rose 6.1%, its highest in five years, and it raised full-year guidance. Dollar Tree is up 8.6% on an EPS beat despite a revenue miss. Against that, MarketWatch reports beef prices that make a roast cost more than a Thanksgiving feast, and CNBC says some food banks see demand above pandemic levels. Strong results from both a discretionary retailer and a discounter point to a stretched but still spending consumer. Consumer confidence at 10:00 AM ET (forecast 92.4, prior 91.7) will add to that picture.

Sanofi agreed to buy Insmed for $41 billion, the biggest biotech deal in nearly three years, to offset patent expirations on a key drug. Insmed is up 14%. Large patent cliffs push big pharma to buy growth rather than build it, and a deal at this price can lift sentiment across the biotech targets that investors see as next. Medtronic is down 3.7% pre-market on a revenue miss with in-line EPS, so the health care read is mixed.

drivers.h: Oil steadies on surplus-versus-shipping tug of war
drivers.t: WTI is at $80.31, up 0.2%, after recovering from early losses as traders weigh Middle East shipping threats against expectations of a global surplus. Bloomberg says resilient Gulf exports, booming output elsewhere and weaker demand are tilting the market toward oversupply. Crude is down 21.1% over one month, which eases energy costs for consumers and tends to ease inflation pressure. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap notes that gasoline has fallen roughly 18% from its May peak.

earnings.t: Best Buy's 6.1% comparable sales growth, its best in five years, and a raised full-year outlook give the pre-market gain a clear fundamental basis.

MarketWatch notes Nvidia still has an investigation to finish, which could keep pressure on the stock that led Monday's rally.
Fiscal worries have already sparked a bond selloff this year, and a budget fight could add to European market stress.
